Melody
mel'o-dy
n. (an agreeable succession of sounds; sweet singing or playing; rendering Hebrew zimrah, Greek psallo in Ephesians 5:19)
From the Greek melodia, from melos, a song or tune, and ode, a song. The English has always meant the tune itself as distinct from the words or the harmony.

Biblical Definition

Melody in the Authorized Version is the sweetness of a tune, and Scripture judges it by what it accompanies. Isaiah gives it to a forgotten harlot city in bitter irony: “Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered” (Isaiah 23:16). Beauty of sound is here a bid for attention by one who has nothing else left, and the prophet is not impressed. Amos gives the divine verdict on melody offered by the unjust: “I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amos 5:23). But the same word describes what God restores to a desolated people: he will make Zion's wilderness like Eden, so that there is found in her “joy and gladness… thanksgiving, and the voice of melody” (Isaiah 51:3). The decisive New Testament use relocates it: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19). The verb is psallo, originally to pluck a string, and Paul names the instrument — the heart. That is not a rejection of audible music but a statement of where the real music is made. A congregation may be in tune and silent in the heart, or plain in sound and full of melody where God hears.

Webster 1828 Definition

An agreeable succession of sounds. Scripture rejects it from the unjust, restores it to a comforted Zion, and in Ephesians relocates it — melody made in the heart, to the Lord.

expand to see more

MELODY, n. [Gr. melodia; melos, a song, and ode, ode.] An agreeable succession of sounds; a succession of sounds so regulated and modulated as to please the ear.

2. To constitute melody, the sounds must be arranged according to the laws of rhythmus, measure, or the due proportion of the movements.

3. Melody differs from harmony, as it consists in the agreeable succession of sounds; harmony consists in their agreeable union.

4. In Scripture, sweetness of sound; as, make sweet melody, Is. 23.

5. Making melody in the heart, Eph. 5; the inward praise of which the voice is the expression.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 23:16 — "Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered."

Amos 5:23 — "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols."

Isaiah 51:3 — "For the LORD shall comfort Zion: he will comfort all her waste places; and he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody."

Ephesians 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;"

Modern Corruption

Sweetness of sound is taken as evidence that worship has been accepted, though Amos records God refusing melody outright — while Ephesians 5:19 is used to excuse silence in the congregation.

expand to see more

The most common misuse runs through feeling: a service that sounded beautiful and moved the affections is assumed to have been received. Amos 5:23 forbids the inference. God there refuses melody from a people whose courts were corrupt, and the refusal is stated as a settled disposition, not a mood. Nothing about a tune can commend a worshipper whose dealings are false, and no amount of skill is a substitute for judgment running down as waters. The opposite abuse takes Paul's in your heart as permission to be silent, as though inward music excused a closed mouth. The same verse commands speaking to yourselves in psalms in its first clause; the heart is where the melody is made, not where it is hidden.

The principle to recover is Isaiah 51:3, which is the sweetest thing said about this word. God does not merely forgive a wasted people; he plants the waste places and puts the voice of melody back among them. That is the gospel order — comfort first, then thanksgiving, then singing. Melody is not the price of God's favour but one of its ordinary fruits, and a heart that has been made like a garden will not stay quiet for long.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zimrah is melody or song of praise, from zamar, to make music. Greek psallo is to pluck a string, and so to sing praise; melos is the tune itself.

expand to see more

Hebrew zimrah (H2172) — melody, a song of praise; from zamar, to strike the strings.

Hebrew neginah (H5058) — a stringed instrument or the music of one; also a taunting song.

Greek psallo (G5567) — to pluck, to twang a string, and hence to sing praise; the verb of Ephesians 5:19.

Greek melos — a tune, a limb; the root of melody, distinct from harmony.

Greek kardia (G2588) — the heart; the instrument Paul names in Ephesians 5:19.

Usage

"Of melody as a bid for notice: make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered (Isaiah 23:16)."

"Of melody refused by God: I will not hear the melody of thy viols (Amos 5:23)."

"Of melody made in the heart: singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19)."
